title: React reconciliation: reuse or remount?
summary: You know components, props and state. Learn how React decides to keep a component or rebuild it: by element type, position and key.
objective: Predict whether a component keeps or loses its state after a re-render, and use keys to reset or preserve it on purpose.

hook.prompt: You type "Ada" into this input, then `isEditing` flips from `false` to `true`. What happens to the text?

options.text: "Ada" stays; only the placeholder changes
The input clears, because a different JSX branch rendered it
options.feedback: That's the common guess. React never sees your branches, only the elements they return.

options.text: React warns that the two inputs need keys
options.feedback: Keys are only expected for children built from arrays. A ternary returns one element, so there's no warning.

hook.explanation: Both branches put an `<input>` in the same spot, so React keeps the same DOM node and just updates its placeholder. Why that is decides everything else in this lesson.

bricks.title: Same type in the same slot: reused
bricks.body: On each render React compares the new element tree with the previous one, **position by position**. At each slot it checks the element **type**: a tag like `'div'`, or the component function itself, compared by reference. Same type: React keeps the DOM node and the component's state and updates its props. Different type: it unmounts that whole subtree, state included, and mounts a fresh one. A `{cond && <X />}` child keeps its slot even when it renders `false`.

term.definition: What an element renders: a tag name string like 'div', or a component function or class, compared by reference.

visual.alt: Three child slots compared before and after a render: Counter to Counter is kept, input to textarea is remounted, and false to Banner mounts a new Banner.
visual.html:
BeforeAfterResult
<Counter><Counter>Kept
<input><textarea>Remounted
false<Banner>Mounted

bricks.prompt: `Counter` shows 3. Then `isFancy` flips from `true` to `false`. What does `Counter` show?

options.text: 0, a fresh `Counter`
3, because `Counter` is the same type in both branches
options.feedback: Right test, wrong level. React compares from the top: the outer slot changed from `div` to `section`, so everything under it is unmounted before `Counter` is ever compared.

options.text: 3, because only the `className` changed
options.feedback: A prop change alone would keep it. But the tag changed too, from `div` to `section`, and a type change at a slot remounts the subtree.

bricks.explanation: The outer element's type changed from `div` to `section`, so React unmounts that whole subtree, including `Counter` and its count, and mounts new ones.

bricks.prompt: The input loses focus after every keystroke. Tap the line that causes it.
bricks.hint: Each keystroke re-runs `SignupForm`. What is new on every run?
bricks.explanation: `EmailField` is declared inside `SignupForm`, so each render creates a new function. A new reference is a new type, so the input remounts. Move `EmailField` to the top level.

bricks.prompt: `Counter` shows 3. Then `isAdmin` flips from `true` to `false`. What does `Counter` show?

options.text: 0, a fresh `Counter`
3, because both are the same `Counter` type
options.feedback: Same type, but not the same slot. The first `Counter` lives in slot 0 and the second in slot 1.

options.text: 3, because the `false` child disappears and `Counter` moves up to slot 0
options.feedback: A `false` child still holds its slot. The new `Counter` stays in slot 1, so nothing matches the old one in slot 0.

bricks.hint: Count the children of the `div`, including the ones that render `false`.
bricks.explanation: Slot 0 goes from `Counter` to `false`, so that `Counter` unmounts. Slot 1 goes from `false` to `Counter`, so a fresh one mounts.

bricks.title: Keys give list items an identity
bricks.body: In a list, position is fragile: insert an item at the top and every row shifts down a slot. A **key** gives each child an identity among its siblings, so React matches old and new children by key instead of index. Same key and type: reused, even if it moved. Key gone: unmounted. New key: mounted. Using the index as the key is no better than position. Put the key on the element `map` returns, and keep it stable.

bricks.prompt: The list shows *Buy milk* (checked) and *Walk dog*. A new todo, *Call mom*, is added at the top. What do you see?

options.text: *Call mom* is checked; *Buy milk* isn't
*Buy milk* is still checked
options.feedback: That needs a key that follows the todo. Here key 0 belonged to *Buy milk* and now belongs to *Call mom*, and the checkbox stays with key 0.

options.text: Nothing is checked, because every row remounts
options.feedback: Keys 0 and 1 existed before, so those rows are reused. Only key 2 is new, and it gets *Walk dog*.

options.text: React warns about duplicate keys
options.feedback: Indexes are unique among the siblings, so there's no warning. That's what makes this bug quiet.

bricks.hint: Which todo has key 0 after the insert?
bricks.explanation: React reuses the row with key 0, checkbox state and all, and only updates its text to *Call mom*. Keying by `todo.id` keeps the check on *Buy milk*.

bricks.prompt: React still warns: "Each child in a list should have a unique key prop." Tap the line where the key belongs.
bricks.hint: Which elements are the siblings inside the `ul`?
bricks.explanation: The siblings React compares are the `<ContactRow>` elements that `map` returns, so the key goes there: `<ContactRow key={c.id} contact={c} />`. A key inside `ContactRow` has no siblings to tell apart.

bricks.prompt: `Counter` shows 3. After each change, does it keep its count?

items.text: Its row moves from first to last in a list keyed by ID
A ternary swaps `<Counter label="A" />` for `<Counter label="B" />` in the same spot
It has `key={Math.random()}` and its parent re-renders

bricks.explanation: Same type with the same key, or in the same slot, keeps state; props don't matter. A changed parent type or a changed key, even a random one, remounts.

bricks.title: Change the key to reset on purpose
bricks.body: Keys work on any element, not only in lists. A new key tells React this is a different instance: the old one unmounts and a fresh one mounts with its initial state. `<ProfileForm key={userId} />` clears the form whenever the user changes, with no effect to sync it. An unmounted instance's state is **destroyed, not stored**. To keep state across a switch, lift it into a parent.

visual.code:
// New userId → new key → fresh ProfileForm
<ProfileForm key={userId} userId={userId} />

bricks.prompt: In a chat app, a half-typed draft stays in `<ChatInput />` when you switch to another contact. What's the cleanest fix?

options.text: `<ChatInput key={contact.id} />`
An effect in `ChatInput` that clears the draft when `contact` changes
options.feedback: It works, but the old draft renders once before the effect clears it, and every new piece of state needs its own reset.

options.text: `<ChatInput key={Math.random()} />`
options.feedback: That resets on switch, but also on every parent re-render, wiping drafts while people type.

options.text: `<ChatInput key="chat" />`
options.feedback: A key that never changes never triggers a reset. The draft still carries over.

bricks.explanation: The key changes exactly when the contact does, so React mounts a fresh `ChatInput` for each conversation, and all its state starts over.

bricks.prompt: Player A's `Scoreboard` shows 5. You switch to B, then back to A. What does A's `Scoreboard` show?

options.text: 5, because key `"A"` brings back A's instance
options.feedback: Keys identify instances that are mounted. When B mounted, A's instance was unmounted and its state destroyed.

options.text: 5, because it's the same type in the same slot
options.feedback: Same type and slot would keep it, but the keys differ, so React treats them as different instances.

options.text: B's score
options.feedback: Different keys mean B's instance isn't reused for A either. A gets a fresh instance.

bricks.hint: What happened to A's instance while B was showing?
bricks.explanation: Switching to B unmounted A and destroyed its state. Switching back mounts a new A from scratch. To keep both scores, lift them into the parent.

challenge.situation: Two bugs in a contacts screen. Rows use `key={index}` and each has an uncontrolled notes input; after a new contact is added and the list re-sorts, notes sit beside the wrong people. And in the side panel, `<EditContact contact={selected} />` keeps the previous contact's unsaved edits.

options.text: Key each row with `c.id`, and render `<EditContact key={selected.id} contact={selected} />`.
options.outcome: Notes follow their contact through any sort, and picking a new contact mounts a clean edit form.

options.text: Key rows with `c.id`, and add an effect in `EditContact` that resets its fields when `contact` changes.
options.outcome: Both bugs go away, but the old edits flash for one render, and each new field needs adding to the reset.

options.text: Use `key={Math.random()}` on the rows and on `EditContact` so everything resets.
options.outcome: Nothing lands on the wrong contact anymore, because nothing survives: every re-render wipes the notes and edits.

options.text: Wrap each row in a `<div>` so React can tell them apart.
options.outcome: Every row gets the same wrapper type, still matched by position. Notes stay on the wrong rows and the panel bug remains.

challenge.explanation: Both bugs are identity bugs. A stable ID lets state follow the right row; a key that changes with the selection resets the form exactly when it should.

takeaways: React keeps a component only when the same type sits in the same slot; a type change remounts the whole subtree.
Declare components at the top level, never inside another component's body.
Key list items with a stable ID from your data, on the element `map` returns, not the index.
Change a key to reset state on purpose; an unmounted component's state is gone for good.
